newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong government lends officials to Tung.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong government lends officials to Tung.

text.p: The departing colonial government extended a helping hand to Hong Kong's future leader on Tuesday by lending him two key officials to guide him through the task of forming his own administration.
Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa is racing against the clock to establish a government ready to take the reins when more than 150 years of British rule ends in 112 days' time.

Hong Kong returns to China at midnight on June 30 and Tung, an experienced businessman but with little political experience, will step into the shoes of Chris Patten, the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong.

Patten and the British have pledged to assist Hong Kong's leader-in-waiting although they have refused to cooperate with a provisional legislature to be installed on July 1 in place of the present elected chamber.

The Hong Kong government said it had agreed to transfer temporarily the secretary for home affairs and the director of information services to Tung's office from Wednesday, which is budget day in Hong Kong.
Home Affairs Secretary Michael Suen would assist Tung in the details of setting up an administration to be grafted on to what will remain from the colonial era.
Public affairs chief Irene Yau, who had been due to retire before the June 30 handover, has agreed to extend her term until the end of June, the government said in a statement.
Tung issued a statement welcoming the secondments and vowed his office would not develop into a shadow power centre.
"I am very pleased with the additional staffing support which is much needed as work builds up in the lead-up to the handover," he said.

"Officers who are seconded to the Chief Executive's office take temporary leave of absence from the government and will work under the direction of, and be accountable to, the Chief Executive. The secondment will end on July 1."
"The important thing for all sides is to make sure my office does not become a second centre of power," he later told reporters.

Tung's move to retain a considerable portion of the colonial government framework has been met with approval in Hong Kong, which China has promised can maintain its capitalist way of life for 50 years beyond the handover.

The Shanghai-born former shipping magnate opted for continuity last month when he announced the reappointment of Hong Kong's top tier civil servants, including the popular and influential chief secretary, Anson Chan.
He also selected two members of Patten's inner cabinet of advisers to serve in his own Executive Council.
He maintained the colonial practice of reserving three seats on the powerful body for Hong Kong's top three civil servants -- including Chan, the civil service chief and Patten's deputy.
But Tung's endorsement of China's plans to dissolve the elected chamber, undoing in a stroke recent democratic reforms instituted by Britain, had stoked anger in some quarters.
The pro-democracy lobby, which won the most support in 1995 elections, the British and their Western allies, have all deplored the plan and urged Tung and China to reconsider.
A provisional legislature has already been selected by the same 400-strong body that chose Tung and meets regularly in China where it is safe from law suits challenging its legality.
The provisional body is expected to serve for about a year until new polls are called under yet-to-be-drafted electoral laws.
